drills.coachNote: Both your knight on e5 and the pawn behind it are under real pressure — Black's knight on d7 and his fianchettoed bishop on g7 both bear down on that square, and once pieces trade off, the recapture pawn on e5 becomes a long-term target for Black's queen from c7. b4 grabbed space on the wrong wing and ignored that, so Black traded on e5, and after dxe5 Qc7 you're babysitting a weak pawn instead of enjoying a winning position — your edge shrank from +2.3 toward equal. drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6 wants to check you and drive your king away from your own pieces, while the c5-d6-e6 pawn trio just needs a crack to start queening. Kd8 put your king on the wrong square — Rb8+ forces Nc8 to block, then c6 gets the passers rolling with your pieces scattered, flipping the position from winning for you (-2.7) to losing (a swing of nearly 8 pawns). Kc8 keeps your king connected to your rook on a5 and knight on e7, so even after c6 Bc4 dxe7 Kc7 Rb7+ you're weathering checks instead of collapsing under them. In these razor-edge pawn races, the exact square your king stands on decides whether checks are annoying or fatal.

drills.coachNote: White's pawn on d5 was just sitting there with nothing covering it — your knight on e7 could grab it clean. Nxd5 wins the pawn immediately, and even though White hits back with Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6, the trades even out and you're no worse off — you just banked the free pawn instead of letting White dictate play. Scan for hanging pawns before making a quiet king move, especially in tight endgames like this.

drills.coachNote: White's king on g1 is nearly boxed in already — your rook on f2 controls the f-file and covers f1, and your queen on c6 has a clear diagonal all the way to g2. That single choice ended the game. Qh7 blocks with the queen instead, keeping f8 defended and offering a trade; after Qxh7+ Kxh7 Bf4 Re8 Rxe8 you reach a simplified, safe position. Qxe5+ traded queens at exactly the wrong moment: after Kxe5 Rfe8+ Kf4 Rd4+ the king survives and your forced mate turned into just 'still better,' a brutal 14-pawn swing from a completely winning position — and you went on to lose the game from there. f5+ kept the attack alive instead, and after Qxf5 Rfe8+ Qe6+ Rxe6 is mate. When the opponent's king is this exposed, don't trade queens — look for the line that keeps checking until it's over.
drills.threat: White's king on e4 has nowhere safe to run — your rook on f8 and queen on g5 can still bring it down directly.

drills.coachNote: Your knight on e4 looked protected by Qe2 sitting behind it, but your own pawn on e3 blocks that file — Black's queen on c6 reaches it cleanly along the c6-e4 diagonal instead. Rac1 developed a rook but left that hanging, so Black just played Qxe4, winning the knight outright, then followed up with c4 and f5 to keep expanding — a 4.5-pawn swing that turned an even game into a lost one. Nd2 simply tucks the knight away to safety first; after Rd8 Nf3 Kg7 Qc2 Rd6 the position stays level. Before a developing move, actually trace which file or diagonal is defending a piece — 'defended' isn't the same as 'defended along an open path.'

Re2 keeps the rook off that file entirely, and after Qd5 Qf4 Qg5+ Qxg5 Bxg5 the queens come off without extra losses. Even when digging for chances in a lost position, count the defenders before grabbing a pawn sitting in front of a queen and rook.

drills.title: vs AnusCarlsen69420 (485) — Caro Kann Defense Advance Variation
drills.coachNote: White's plan is simple: swap the bishop on g5 for your knight on f6, then meet the recapture with Qh5+, and h6 hands him exactly the extra weakness he needs to make that check sting. That's what happened — Bxf6 exf6 Qh5+ g6 left your king stuck in the center behind a battered, holey kingside, roughly a 3-pawn swing even though you went on to win the game anyway. g6 instead prepares Bg7, fighting for the long diagonal and covering f6 and h5 without inviting the trade on good terms; after Bd3 Bg7 O-O Nbd7 Nf3 you get a completely normal, solid Advance Caro-Kann. Before castling, be careful with pawn moves near your own king — a move that looks useful can just hand over the check the opponent wanted.

drills.coachNote: Black's queen on h4 already had your bishop on h6 in its sights, undefended, and that was the thing you needed to deal with. Qxb7 grabbed a pawn but ignored it — Black played Qxh6!, taking the bishop for free, and after Rad1 g5 Qd7 you'd handed back most of a five-plus pawn advantage chasing a pawn instead of protecting the bigger piece. Bg7+! was the answer: it uses the hanging bishop with check instead of just losing it — Rxg7 is forced, then Qxc8+! wins the rook on c8, and after Qd8 Qxd8+ Nxd8 you're trading into a completely winning endgame. When a piece is hanging, look for a way to give it up on your own terms — with interest.
